title: User Execution: Malicious Copy and Paste
shortTitle: User Execution: Malicious Copy and Paste
summary: Malicious copy and paste is the sub-technique where the victim personally runs the adversary's command, having been told that it is a fix. The published pattern, often called ClickFix, is a web page or document that shows a fake error, a failed download or a verification prompt, then instructs the visitor to open a terminal or the Windows Run dialog and paste a line of text to resolve it. The pasted text is frequently encoded or split so that the visible screen does not resemble a command, and the resulting process is started by the user's own terminal or run dialog, which means it inherits valid user context and produces no downloaded executable for a mail gateway to judge. Because the user is the one who acts, the technique sidesteps attachment filtering, browser sandboxing around downloads, and warnings aimed at files. The strongest detection signals are behavioural rather than file based: a shell, scripting host or run dialog appearing as the parent of a network utility or a remote monitoring tool, a single command line containing both an encoded blob and a network address, short lived child processes from a terminal, and the clipboard history or browser session that preceded it.

beginner.definition: This means the attacker asks you to copy a piece of text and paste it into a terminal. The page claims the text will fix an error. Running it actually starts the attacker's code. You do the last step yourself, which is the trick.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your computer trusts commands you type or paste yourself more than files from the internet. Email and browser filters look for files and links, not for text you paste. The instructions often look like normal technical support advice. Because you started the command, warnings are less likely to appear.
howItWorks: You visit a page, or open a file, that shows a fake error message.
The page says the download failed, or asks you to prove you are human, and offers a fix.
It tells you to press a key combination to open the Run box or a terminal window.
You copy a line of text from the page and paste it in, sometimes pressing enter as instructed.
The text is often encoded so its real purpose is not obvious on screen.
Your own terminal runs the command, which fetches and starts the attacker's tool.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat noticeboard saying the boiler is broken. A note tells residents to press the service button and read the code to an engineer. A neighbour follows the note and passes on the four digit code. Later, a stranger uses that code to walk in. The note was the attack, and the resident did the work.
takeaways: Never paste commands from a website or message into a terminal, whatever the page claims.
A terminal, run box or script host starting a network tool is a high priority alert.
If a page tells you to open a terminal to fix an error, that alone is a warning sign.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from opening a malicious file or clicking a link.
Describe the ClickFix pattern of a fake error or CAPTCHA that asks for a pasted command.
Explain why actions started by the user are trusted more and detected less.
Identify process lineage and command line evidence that reveals a pasted command.
Describe user education messages that make a terminal instruction a recognised alarm.
